cards.front: In the leaf-pile bathtub model of a forest, which group is the tap and which group is the drain?
cards.back: Producers are the tap: they pour new leaves in each autumn. Decomposers are the drain: they turn the pile back into carbon dioxide, water and nutrients.
cards.quote: Producers pour new leaves in each autumn, and consumers carry some matter along. Decomposers drain the pile back into carbon dioxide, water and nutrients that producers use again.

cards.front: In the bathtub model of a forest floor, when does the leaf pile stop growing?
cards.back: When the drain takes out as much as falls in each year.
cards.quote: The pile stops growing when the drain takes out as much as falls in each year.

cards.front: In a peat bog, cold or waterlogged ground nearly stops decomposers. Using the bathtub model, what happens to the pile of dead plants?
cards.back: It keeps growing. The drain is almost shut, so little is removed while new plant matter keeps falling in.
cards.why: The pile levels off only when the drain removes as much as falls in.
cards.quote: In peat bogs, cold or waterlogged ground nearly stops the drain, and dead plants keep piling up.

cards.front: A {{c1::producer}} captures energy from sunlight and stores it in sugar (glucose).
cards.quote: A producer captures energy from sunlight and stores it in sugar (glucose) built from carbon dioxide and water
cards.section: Explain: three jobs in an ecosystem

cards.front: A {{c1::consumer}} is an organism that gets energy by eating other organisms.
cards.quote: A consumer is an organism that gets energy by eating other organisms.
cards.section: Explain: three jobs in an ecosystem

cards.front: What are the main decomposers in a forest?
cards.quote: The main decomposers are fungi and bacteria.
cards.section: Explain: three jobs in an ecosystem

cards.front: In a forest food web, a deer eats acorns and a fox eats a seed-eating mouse. Which order of consumer is each animal?
cards.back: The deer is a first-order consumer. The fox is a second-order consumer. The order counts steps from the producer.
cards.quote: A deer eating acorns is a first-order consumer. A fox eating a seed-eating mouse is a second-order consumer.
cards.section: Explain: three jobs in an ecosystem

cards.front: What is respiration, and is it the same as breathing?
cards.back: No. Respiration is how cells release the energy in food.
cards.quote: Respiration is not breathing. It is how cells release the energy in food
cards.section: Explain: the drain in the bathtub

cards.front: When forest decomposers break down a leaf, why does much of its carbon end up in the air?
cards.back: Most forest decomposers' cells use oxygen for respiration and give off carbon dioxide and water, and carbon is a large share of a dry leaf.
cards.quote: in you and most forest decomposers it uses oxygen. Carbon is a large share of a dry leaf
cards.section: Explain: the drain in the bathtub

cards.front: Where do the nutrients in a dead leaf go when decomposers break it down?
cards.back: Decomposers return them to the soil, or to the water in a stream, where producers can use them again.
cards.quote: Decomposers return them to the soil, or to the water in a stream.
cards.section: Explain: the drain in the bathtub

cards.front: In the simple leaf-pile model, 1 autumn's worth of leaves falls each year and decomposers remove half the pile over the next year. The pile just after leaf fall is 1.75 in year 3. What is it in year 4?
cards.back: About 1.9 autumns' worth. Half of 1.75 is 0.875, plus 1 new autumn's worth is 1.875.
cards.quote: Each new pile is half the old one plus 1. In year 2, half of 1 is 0.5, plus 1 makes 1.5
cards.section: How tall does the pile get?

cards.front: In a simple model of cold, dry years, decomposers remove only a quarter of the pile each year, and 1 autumn's worth falls each year. Does the pile stop growing, and at about how many autumns' worth?
cards.back: It levels off near 4 autumns' worth, because a quarter of 4 is 1, which matches what falls in. A slower drain means a taller pile, not an endless one.
cards.quote: The pile stops near 2, because half of 2 is 1.
cards.section: How tall does the pile get?

cards.front: {{c1::Abiotic factors}} are nonliving conditions such as temperature and moisture.
cards.quote: Abiotic factors, nonliving conditions such as temperature and moisture, help set how fast the drain runs
cards.section: How tall does the pile get?

cards.front: In a forest, most of the fungi and bacteria are killed by a soil poison. Predict what happens to the dead leaves and to the plants over many years.
cards.back: Dead leaves pile up, and fewer nutrients return to the soil, so plants may grow less over time. The drain is clogged.
cards.quote: Fewer decomposers (a clogged drain): dead leaves pile up.

cards.front: A homeowner rakes away every fallen leaf from the yard each autumn. Predict the effect on the soil and on decomposers.
cards.back: Nutrients are removed with the leaves, and decomposers lose their food. Leaving leaves in a corner, or composting, feeds decomposers instead.
cards.quote: Raking away every leaf removes nutrients.

cards.front: A forest is cleared. Using the tap and drain idea, explain how this could harm producers, plant eaters and decomposers.
cards.back: Clearing removes producers, a weaker tap. Plant eaters have less food, and fewer new leaves fall, so decomposers lose the litter that feeds them.
cards.why: It rests on the rule that changes to one group reach the others.
cards.quote: Clearing a forest removes producers and the new leaf litter that feeds decomposers.

cards.front: In the Weimer Run leaf bags, 41.2 percent of the starting mass was left at the lower site after 24 months. What percent of the mass was gone?
cards.back: 58.8 percent. Subtract the percent left from 100: 100 - 41.2 = 58.8.
cards.quote: After 24 months, 41.2 percent was left there, against 47.8 percent.
cards.section: Elaborate: two years in a bag of leaves

cards.front: In the leaf-bag data, the lower site went from 68.9 to 70.9 percent mass left between months 1 and 8. Why might mass left go up when leaves are breaking down?
cards.back: Different bags were weighed each time, so values bounce around. A small rise does not mean leaves gained mass.
cards.quote: Different bags were weighed each time, so values bounce around
cards.section: Elaborate: two years in a bag of leaves

cards.front: Design a test of whether moist soil makes leaves break down faster than dry soil, using leaves, cups of soil and a balance. Name the variables and the control.
cards.back: Independent variable: moist or dry soil. Dependent variable: dry leaf mass left after 4 weeks. Control: cups of dry soil with no water added. Constants: leaf kind, 2.0 grams per cup, soil, cup size, temperature. Five cups of each, then compare means.
cards.quote: Water can also wash material out of leaves without any decomposers, so this test alone cannot show how much of the loss came from decomposers.

cards.front: A student says an earthworm is a decomposer, another says it is food for robins. Who is right?
cards.back: The jobs overlap: an earthworm helps break down dead leaves and is also food for robins. Some books call it a detritivore.
cards.quote: An earthworm helps break down dead leaves and is also food for robins.

cards.front: In the Weimer Run leaf bags, about 40 to 46 percent of mass was gone after one year but only 12 to 13 percent more in the second. What could explain the slowing?
cards.back: Breakdown may slow as the easy parts of a leaf are used up, though the weather also differed between years.
cards.quote: That fits breakdown slowing down once the easy parts of a leaf are used up.
cards.section: Why a real pile is not exactly 2 autumns

cards.front: The Weimer Run leaf bags had mesh holes about 1 millimeter wide. How does that affect using their rate for a whole forest floor?
cards.back: Earthworms and millipedes could not get in, so the bag rate is probably slower than on a real forest floor. It is a useful rate for leaves in bags only.
cards.quote: Worms, kept out by the mesh, would probably speed things up.
cards.section: Why a real pile is not exactly 2 autumns
